body.text: Why brush-applied stain matters in this climate

Sprayed stain looks fast and even from a distance, but it mostly sits on the surface of the wood rather than soaking into it. In a climate like Kitchener-Waterloo's, where the wood goes through repeated freeze and thaw cycles all winter and intense UV through the summer, a surface-level coating is exactly the kind of finish that cracks and peels first. Restore My Deck brushes every stain job by hand instead. Brushing pushes the product into the wood grain, into end grain at board edges, and into fastener holes where moisture likes to collect, which are the areas that fail first when a deck is under-protected. The result is a finish that penetrates rather than sits, so it wears down gradually over a couple of seasons instead of flaking off in sheets.

We work primarily with two premium, oil-based, VOC-compliant stain lines: Ready Seal and Penofin Verde. Ready Seal is known for going on easily and penetrating deeply, which suits both pressure-treated pine and cedar and holds up well through our region's humid summers. Penofin Verde is formulated to nourish the wood as it protects it and comes in a wide range of colours, which makes it a good fit when you are trying to match an existing deck colour or coordinate with siding and trim. Both products are plant-safe and low-VOC, and both are chosen specifically because they age by fading rather than peeling, so a maintenance coat later is a simple re-application rather than a strip-and-redo.

items: Transparent: shows the most wood grain, lowest UV protection, needs reapplication most often
Semi-transparent: our most popular choice, balances visible grain with solid weather protection
Semi-solid: hides more surface wear and older wood imperfections while still showing some texture
Solid: full colour coverage, best for older or heavily weathered wood, closest to a paint-like finish

body.text: Most homeowners in Kitchener-Waterloo land on semi-transparent, since it protects well against both UV and moisture while still letting the wood look like wood. Pressure-treated pine tends to take stain a bit more unevenly than cedar because of its tighter grain and manufacturing chemicals, so we sometimes recommend a slightly heavier sheen on pine decks to even out the finish, while cedar's natural grain often looks best under a lighter transparent or semi-transparent coat.
Preparation is what makes staining last

Staining is only as good as the surface underneath it. Every project starts with a thorough clean using wood-safe detergents to remove dirt, mildew and any remnants of previous stain or sealant, since staining over grime traps it under the new finish and shortens its lifespan. On decks with rough or weathered boards we add an 80-grit buff sanding pass before staining, which opens the grain further and gives the oil-based stain more surface area to penetrate. If your deck also needs structural repairs, our /deck-repair-and-maintenance service handles that ahead of staining, and if it needs a full clean, sand and stain treatment together, /deck-restoration bundles all three.
Most staining projects are finished in about two days including drying time; larger decks typically take three.

In Southwestern Ontario, late spring through early fall gives the most reliable staining conditions, since the oil needs stable temperatures and low humidity to cure fully before rain or dew arrives. We avoid staining right before a forecasted cold snap or heavy rain, both of which are common in our shoulder seasons, and we schedule drying time generously to account for the region's humidity swings. Staining a deck in the fall before winter arrives gives the wood a protective coat heading into the freeze-thaw months, which is one of the most requested times of year for us.

Because our stains fade rather than peel, a maintenance re-stain every 2 to 4 years keeps most decks looking good without needing a full restoration in between. If your existing stain has faded evenly and the wood underneath is still sound, a straightforward re-stain is usually all that is needed, and we will tell you plainly if we think you need more. faqs.q: Why do you brush-apply stain instead of spraying it?
faqs.a: Brushing works the stain into the wood grain, end cuts and fastener holes, which are the areas that fail first in our freeze-thaw climate. Spraying leaves more product sitting on the surface, where it is more likely to crack and peel.

faqs.q: What stain brands do you use?
faqs.a: We primarily use Ready Seal and Penofin Verde, both premium, VOC-compliant, oil-based stains chosen for how evenly they penetrate and fade over time without peeling.

faqs.q: Which stain sheen is most popular?
faqs.a: Semi-transparent is our most requested option because it balances visible wood grain with strong UV and moisture protection, which suits both pressure-treated pine and cedar decks in this climate.

faqs.q: How often should I restain my deck?
faqs.a: Most decks need a maintenance re-stain every 2 to 4 years depending on sun exposure and wood type, with a fuller restoration recommended every 5 to 7 years.

faqs.q: Do you stain both pressure-treated pine and cedar decks?
faqs.a: Yes. Pine and cedar absorb stain differently, so we adjust sheen recommendations and application technique to suit each wood type.
